newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup-A non-reforming budget.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup-A non-reforming budget.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV Political Correspondent)
Just over three weeks to Peter Costello's budget Mark II and a "ho hum" affair he's privately predicting it will be.
But a big yawn is not what business, big or small, is after.

John Howard went to Brisbane during the week. Queenslanders seem to have a genetic disposition to treat politicians from the south like a bad smell. And it was no different for the Prime Minister who got a particularly in-your-face "welcome" at a Liberal party lunch function from state president Bob Tucker.
After lecturing Howard on Wik and Mal (Colston, that is), Tucker turned his attention to next month's budget.
"I hope the coming budget will continue the reform process," implored Tucker.
"Much more needs to be done if small business is to play its rightful role in creating the jobs that we need ... to get this country really moving.
"The patience of the business community and especially the small business supporters right around this state is not unlimited," Tucker told the Prime Minister.
The initial signs are that Tucker and other impatient members of the business community should not be holding their breath in expectation of a reform budget.
Mid-term housekeeping seems more the order of the day.
The government clearly is not planning to attempt anything approaching last year's A$7.0 billion effort in cutting spending.
In fact many ministers are obviously miffed that the A$1.6 billion shortfall in company tax receipts is forcing them to shake their portfolios once again in a search for a bit more loose change.

Telstra's A$3.0 billion special dividend will affect the headline budget result, but not the structural deficit and so is unlikely to have much impact on ERC's (expenditure review committee) penny pinching exercise.

Howard is also signalling privately that the big reform efforts for this term are already in place. The view from the Oval Office -- or perhaps that should be Kirribilli -- is that they simply need either:
-- Developing, like work-for-the-dole;
-- Realising, like the planned new job placement agency; or
-- Fine tuning, where health is a key example.

The Productivity Commission provided Michael Wooldridge with a fine pretext for an overdue shake-up of the health management system. But after a comprehensive review of the private health insurance sector, the Health Minister rejected well-argued recommendations for an inquiry into the system itself.
Also rejected was an overdue examination of the community rating principle whose actuarial imperfections have the system teetering.

Wooldridge might like to start from the ground up -- to allow the introduction of competitive principles which would impose cost disciplines across the entire sector -- but he's been hobbled by Howard's literal commitment to the coalition's 1996 election promise to retain Medicare and community rating.
That meant there was little more he could do than tinker with the existing system -- doing nothing to repair its inherent creaks and cracks.

The government decided to fiddle with community rating, but in ways that are unlikely to make it more attractive to the uninsured. Why join a private fund if you're going to be charged more for late entry or have key services denied.
Wooldridge himself could not guarantee the changes would increase fund membership above its current uneconomic level.
It's an admission that does not sit well with his claim that "... the long-term viability of Medicare depends on a stronger private health insurance industry".

If the A$1.6 billion company tax blow-out was bad news for a government looking for relaxation and comfort in its second year budget, there was more bad news from this week when The Australian Financial Review reported a shortfall in tax office receipts from small business.
The Tax Office denied the shortfall but conceded: "There is a perception that non-compliance with the taxation laws through the cash economy is a significant problem ..."
Shades of bottom of the harbour.

The tax system depends less on rigorous enforcement than on community acceptance. If it becomes the entrenched community view that unfair tax planning and avoidance are rampant the whole system suffers.
Howard may come to rue the day he failed to seize the opportunity for a comprehensive review of tax a la Wallis.

Not just because the tax system is falling into disrepute, but because of the inability of a creaking and porous set of taxes, rebates, subsidies and exemptions to provide the receipts even a cost-conscious government needs.
Howard and Costello's gamble is that the policy initiatives already undertaken or underway will see them through to victory at the next election.
That's why "ho hum" is what the Treasurer hopes the May 13 budget will be. Bob Tucker is likely to be disappointed.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
